analysis.one_liner: Opened protected offshore and Alaskan lands to oil drilling and suspended federal gas taxes when prices crossed a benchmark.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors, never received a committee vote, and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill, introduced by Rep. Ron Paul, was pitched as a way to lower gasoline prices after gas neared $3–$4 a gallon. It would have opened the Outer Continental Shelf and the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to oil and gas leasing, revoked presidential withdrawals of offshore areas, and made new environmental impact statements immune from lawsuits in federal court. It also would have given oil refiners generous new tax breaks, suspended the federal highway fuel tax whenever average retail gas exceeded $3.00 per gallon (reimbursing highway trust funds from general taxpayer money), raised business mileage deductions to at least 70 cents per mile, and let the President extend normal trade relations to Russia and Kazakhstan. It was referred to three committees, picked up no cosponsors, and never came to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers and truckers would have paid less at the pump while the tax suspension was active, since the federal fuel tax would stop being collected whenever average retail gasoline topped $3.00 per gallon. Oil and gas companies would have gained access to areas long kept off-limits for drilling, including the Arctic refuge and much of the Outer Continental Shelf, and refiners would have gotten the ability to immediately deduct their full investment in new refinery construction plus faster depreciation on refining equipment. Russian and Kazakh exporters would have gained normal trade relations, which the bill argued would widen non-Arab oil supply.

how_it_helps.text: It would have suspended the federal tax on highway motor fuels whenever the weekly national average retail price for regular gasoline exceeded $3.00 per gallon, with highway trust funds reimbursed from general Treasury funds so programs kept their money.

It would have repealed the statutory bans that keep the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain and offshore oil and gas leasing off-limits, and revoked existing presidential withdrawals of Outer Continental Shelf areas from drilling.

It would have let oil refiners immediately expense 100% of qualified refinery investments and classify petroleum refining property as 5-year property, reducing their tax bills for building new refining capacity.

It would have raised the optional business mileage deduction to at least 70 cents per mile, and during any tax-suspension period extended the business-rate deduction to medical, moving, and charitable driving.
It would have authorized the President to extend normal trade relations to Russia and Kazakhstan, ending the application of the Jackson-Vanik provisions of the Trade Act of 1974 to those countries.

analysis.who_pays: General taxpayers would have covered the lost fuel-tax revenue, since the bill required general Treasury appropriations to make highway and related trust funds whole whenever the tax was suspended — a recurring, unbudgeted cost whenever gas averaged over $3. The public would also have borne the environmental cost of opening the Arctic refuge and the Outer Continental Shelf to drilling and of losing the ability to sue over mandatory environmental impact statements, since those statements would no longer be subject to judicial review.

drawbacks.text: Opening the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain and revoking presidential withdrawals of offshore areas would have exposed previously protected lands and waters to oil and gas development, and the bill offered no new environmental review or public process in exchange.

It would have made mandatory environmental impact statements immune from judicial review, removing the main legal avenue citizens and groups have to challenge federal actions under the National Environmental Policy Act.

The fuel-tax suspension was designed to switch on automatically whenever average retail gas exceeded $3.00 per gallon — a level prices reached in 2005–2006 — so it would have repeatedly diverted revenue from dedicated transportation funding onto the general taxpayer and the deficit.

Economists generally note that new offshore and Arctic production takes years to reach market, so the drilling provisions would have delivered little near-term relief at the pump, which was the bill's stated purpose.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The immediate consumer benefit — a fuel-tax holiday above $3.00 a gallon — was real but expensive, funded by general taxpayers rather than the fuel tax itself, and larger deductions for business driving would mainly have benefited filers who itemize business driving costs. The supply-side provisions aimed at lower prices over the long run, but the price of that was opening the Arctic refuge and the Outer Continental Shelf to drilling and stripping citizens' ability to sue over environmental impact statements. The bill packaged a modest, costly consumer tax break with large concessions to oil producers and refiners and a major rollback of environmental review, without addressing that its own text acknowledged unpriced causes of high prices.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and then to subcommittees, got zero cosponsors, and never got a committee or floor vote before the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Paul introduced the bill on October 6, 2005, framing it as a response to gasoline prices that had risen to as much as over $4 per gallon.
The House referred it to the Ways and Means, Resources, and Financial Services Committees, which sent it to their Energy and Mineral Resources, Trade, and Monetary Policy subcommittees.
No committee ever voted it out, and no cosponsors joined the bill.
The bill died in committee when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The lands and waters the bill would have opened — the Arctic refuge and protected Outer Continental Shelf areas — stayed protected, and citizens kept their right to sue over federal environmental reviews. Oil and refiners gained nothing from the bill's death, but neither did taxpayers face the recurring cost of a fuel-tax suspension backfilled from general funds.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no other member cosponsored the bill, so the partisan split was never tested; it died quietly with its Republican sponsor alone.

industries.note: The bill would have given producers access to the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and removed bans and presidential withdrawals on Outer Continental Shelf leasing, plus normal trade relations with Russia and Kazakhstan that the bill's findings tie to broader oil supply. Producers would have gained new reserves, while the promised consumer price relief would have taken years to materialize, if at all, and the public would have borne the environmental risk.

Refiners could have immediately expensed 100% of qualifying refinery investment and used 5-year depreciation on refining property, substantially lowering their taxes on new capacity. To the extent that spurs more refining capacity, the theory goes, tighter gasoline supply margins would ease.

The bill's own findings named trucking as hard-hit by fuel costs; truckers would have benefited directly from the fuel-tax suspension during high-price periods and from the higher 70-cent business mileage deduction.

industries.industry: Highway trust fund programs (state transportation departments and construction)
industries.note: Fuel-tax suspension would have cut trust fund receipts, but the bill required general Treasury appropriations to make the funds whole, so road programs were backfilled — at the cost of shifting the burden onto general taxpayers and the deficit.

The bill would have repealed ANWR protections, revoked presidential offshore withdrawals, and removed judicial review of mandatory environmental impact statements, eliminating the main legal check on federal energy permitting. Conservation groups and citizens living near affected lands and coasts would have lost their principal legal remedies.
